extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners evaluating 35 U.S.C. §101 eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Apply the MPEP/Alice two-step framework to determine whether a patent claim is statutorily eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 by identifying judicial exceptions and evaluating whether the claim integrates them into a practical application or adds a sufficient inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: Statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim falls within any statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim reciting steps or acts of receiving, converting, and using a DNN is a process (a series of steps or acts), which is a statutory category. See MPEP 2106.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A, Prong One: Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception (set forth or described in the claim) such as an abstract idea (mathematical concept, mental process) or law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim language includes mathematical operations (e.g., STFT, V = fθ(X)) or mental processes (e.g., partitioning into clusters that could be done mentally), the claim recites a judicial exception. See MPEP 2106.04, subsection II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts vs mental processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which grouping(s) of abstract ideas the claim limitations fall into (e.g., mathematical concepts, mental processes) and treat them appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical concepts include specific transforms and formulas (e.g., STFT, embedding formula). Mental processes include concepts performed in the human mind such as observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion (e.g., detecting anomalies by human observation). When multiple limitations fall within the same grouping, consider them together as a single abstract idea. See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) and II.B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not parse multiple abstract ideas unless clearly distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid parsing a claim into multiple separate judicial exceptions unless it is clear the claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., law of nature and an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly in claims involving abstract ideas, consider limitations together rather than analyzing separately. See MPEP 2106.04, subsection II.B (discussing Bilski v. Kappos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental process practical-performability test
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is a 'mental process' if it can be practically performed in the human mind by observation, evaluation, judgment, or opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'detecting one or more anomalies in network traffic' is a mental process because a human could observe network traffic data and use evaluation/judgment to detect anomalies. By contrast, detecting a source address and dropping/ blocking packets in real time cannot be practically performed in the human mind. See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2), subsection III.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A, Prong Two: Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application by identifying additional elements beyond the exception and evaluating them individually and in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform (1) identification of any additional elements beyond the judicial exception, and (2) assessment of those elements alone and together to determine if the claim integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP 2106.04(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to computer or technical field indicates integration
rubrics_metrics.description: One indicator that a claim integrates an exception into a practical application is that the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or another technology/technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate improvements, the specification must set forth a technical improvement and the claim must reflect that disclosed improvement. See MPEP 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a). Example: steps that detect source addresses, drop packets, and block future traffic can reflect an improvement in network intrusion detection and thus integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer or generic component recitation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting use of a computer or a generic component (e.g., 'a deep neural network') without details can amount to no more than mere instructions to apply the judicial exception on a generic computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the claim: (1) recites only the idea of a solution/outcome without details, (2) invokes computers/machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process, and (3) is particular or general in its application. If the claim lacks detail about how the component operates to solve a technical problem, it likely represents mere instructions to apply the exception. See MPEP 2106.05(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (data gathering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that amount to mere data gathering or are recited at a high level of generality may be 'insignificant extra-solution activity' and not enough to integrate the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'receiving a mixed speech signal' at high generality is necessary to use the mathematical calculation but imposes no meaningful limit and is considered insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP 2106.05(g)). Such findings should be re-evaluated at Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular field-of-use linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting a particular field of use (e.g., 'network traffic') can be a link to a technological environment but does not necessarily integrate the exception into a practical application by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recitation of 'network traffic' generally links the abstract idea to a particular field of use (see MPEP 2106.05(h)), but additional technical improvement/particularity is typically required to show integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited judicial exception by adding an inventive concept via additional elements or their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-evaluate whether extra-solution activities are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field (MPEP 2106.05(g)). If additional elements are merely conventional or routine, or are only instructions to implement the exception on generic computers, they do not provide an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the specification's disclosed technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the specification describes a technical improvement, the claim must include limitations that reflect that improvement to avoid being directed to the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the disclosure may describe an improvement achieved by partitioning embeddings, clustering, and synthesizing signals, but a claim that only requires determining embedding vectors without the other reflective limitations fails to reflect the disclosed improvement and may be ineligible. See MPEP 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation standard: Broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim terms according to their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification (MPEP 2111). For example, 'receiving' a mixed speech signal could encompass receiving via a microphone in a user device or other sensors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-mental technical operations are not abstract mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that cannot be practically performed in the human mind (e.g., converting masked clusters into time-domain waveforms, real-time packet dropping) are not mental processes and may support eligibility when they reflect a technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: synthesizing speech waveforms from masked clusters (inverse STFT) is not practically performable mentally and is not a method of organizing human activity; such steps can be considered technical operations for eligibility analysis.
